reason: Attacked and survived. I did not take the verifier's word for it: I pulled three independent texts and read the passage in each. Project Gutenberg 34901 carries the sentence verbatim at line 1731, inside chapter II, whose heading the file prints as CHAPTER II / OF THE LIBERTY OF THOUGHT AND DISCUSSION at line 1009, so the chapter locator is right. I then checked it against two 1859 scans the verifier never opened: Internet Archive onlibertyxero00milluoft (John W. Parker and Son, West Strand) and onliberty03millgoog (the Second Edition, also 1859). Both print “He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.” on page 67 under the running head THOUGHT AND DISCUSSION, with the same comma. The 1859 in the source line is therefore earned rather than assumed. Attribution is not in doubt and the misattribution list does not touch it: the Mill trap on that list is the “triumph of evil” line from the 1867 St Andrews address, a different text. shipped.js: not banned, zero of three for the year, nothing shipped and nothing near. In scope (1859, philosophy, publishable, no content warning) and squarely on Wisdom and Counsel. Source line leads with the name, no dash, no straight quote, 89 characters; tag Philosophy is the form of the work. One cosmetic defect, in the evidence field only and not on the card: the verifier places the sentence “in the paragraph beginning What Cicero practised as the means of forensic success”, but that clause is mid-paragraph in every text I opened; the paragraph begins earlier, at the balance between two sets of conflicting reasons. That misdescribes the evidence, not the citation.
betterCitation: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, chapter II, Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion (1859), p. 67
